title: MKS Pedal in Tokorozawa, Japan: Value from Process – John Watson
content:
Continuing our tour of heritage Japanese manufacturers, we visit the final bosses of pedals at MKS in Tokorozawa, Japan. When Cari and John walked away from this Shop Visit, they had one thing on their minds: value perceived from witnessing the process. Read on for another collaborative post between The Radavist and Slow Spin Society, presented by Sim Works…

Paul, Cari, and Masashi

Sim Works Road Trip: MKS

Kimura-san and I thousand-yard stared out the rainy windshield in his car, waiting at a red light after leaving the MKS facilities, about to embark on our drive to Zushi, Japan, for a day of downtime. His wipers were making a sound one might hear from a robot dog in an Akihabara toy shop. “Wow” is all I could say. Masashi laughed in his very astute Japanese way. “Yeah.” All of us in the car – Paul from Slow Spin, Cari, Masashi, and me – sat in silence, listening to the mew of the windshield wiper.

Value from process was swirling through my head. Being on the inside of bike media has allowed me certain privileges I’ve tried hard not to take for granted. One of which is being an observer of the manufacturing process around the globe. But nothing had prepared me for my perspective shift on pedals after visiting MKS in Tokorozawa, Japan.

MKS Pedals

Those 1983 Suntour XC pedals I have on my Steve Potts? Those loose ball pedals that still shine like rims in a Pall Wall music video? They were made here. In the thousands. With each set being touched by a dozen hands at this very factory. All those shiny 1984 Specialized Pista pedals that were the exact same as the MKS SVX Keirin pedals. Made here too. Many of the same workers who produced those pedals are still employed by MKS today.

The scars on my shins from BMX Foot Jaws pedals from my youth’s Mongoose BMX bike were tingling as I picked up a NOS pair, in blue, of course, to photograph from the MKS archives, nestled in a showroom with the most epic soft-box light.

BIKE

Yuba-san comes over, with a laugh, and shows me the brand’s first pedal model, aptly named “BIKE.” “I wonder how they came up with the name?” He said with a smile. The hefty pedals landed on the glass with a thunkkkk. We’d just finished burgers and coffee from Japan’s burger fast food chain, Mos. And Yuba was eager to get started on the factory tour but was being incredibly patient with Paul and me.

Moving throughout MKS’ facilities on that rainy day, Kenta Yubamoto (Yuba-san) stepped through the factory with a cool, collected demeanor, excited to showcase the factory he was working towards running, which is currently under the helm of his father-in-law and president, Toshiyuki Ogino. Ogino-san was recovering from a cold and couldn’t join us for our tour, but Yuba-san, representing the next generation in Japanese manufacturing, was doing a phenomenal job.

Knowing what we’d geek out at, he began the day with an exclamation: “We should go to the heat-treating facilities now. You’ll like it.”

We walked through giant celadon colored doors, a familiar hue in factories in Japan. My color theory classes during my architecture education bounced back into the forefront of my memory. This seafoam color was intentionally selected for factories in the 1940s. It helps reduce visual fatigue and improves worker safety and efficiency. And MKS was covered in it. Floor to ceiling.

Kenta Yubamoto and Toshiyuki Ogino. Ogino-san (right) showed up at the end of the workday and our tour for a photo…

Mikashima Industrial Company Limited

Before we continue, it’s important to reiterate what the word legacy means: an impact handed down from a person, predecessor, or historical period. Japan is no stranger to manufacturing. Nor to the bicycle. Your favorite component groupset, be it from Suntour or Shimano, arose from the east with the rising sun. And those pedals that just won’t quit, most likely were made behind these very walls.

MKS (Mikashima Industrial Company Limited) was not founded by a single individual; instead, it was established as a company managed and operated by the Ogino family. Toshiyuki Ogino is the current president, a classic Japanese businessman with an austere yet friendly demeanor. His son-in-law, Kenta Yubamoto, aka Yuba-san, acts as the vice president.

The factory in Tokorozawa was built in 1943 and was used to make airplane parts for the war. In the post-war Japanese manufacturing boom, the Ogino family bought it and immediately switched to manufacturing bicycle pedals in 1946 with its first model, the “BIKE.” Designed for mamachari bicycles, these hefty, 700+ gram pedals launched a brand that still stands today.

Unlike the Nitto factory, the MKS facilities look properly maintained and have been brought up to modern standards in terms of lighting, with a façade barely showing its age.

Fire, Fire!

Back to the tour Yuba-san was starting with us. In the heat treatment facility. A pilot flame spurts out of a giant steel vault-like machine. As a loud alarm sounds, a small trolley brings in racks of pedal spindles. Yuba takes a step back.

Please allow this brief aside from a gaijin, a foreigner, but Japan seemingly has no OSHA. Or if they do, it is more relaxed than the regulations I’m more accustomed to. Sure, there’s a line painted on the ground here, but no heat shield, and no one is wearing eye or ear protection, either. My innate self preservation instincts tells me I should step back a few feet.

The door to the heat treatment furnace opens, and flames bellow out as this beast of metal engulfs crates of freshly formed pedal parts. Hairs on my hands feel warm and lightly singe, dancing as I focus my lens on the inferno. Inside, these parts will endure 900 degrees Celsius for 2 hours and move through numerous phases. Quenching: after the fire, parts receive an oil bath at 55 Celsius, resulting in harder but more brittle parts. Annealing: this brings back material flexibility so it is not brittle anymore. This treatment would not work if the parts were oxidized, so the fire gets rid of all the oxygen in the chamber and creates a high carbon density layer to give the spindles strength.

After the heat treatment, we begin the normal tour, starting with a cold forge.

Coil Fed Cold Forging

Taking a step back, MKS has a series of cold forging machines: two smaller ones for things like cone washers, and a larger one, fed by a 100-meter-long coil of Japanese steel. This machine cuts the coiled steel into spindle lengths and then pounds them into shape over five cycles. This includes shaping the spindles and forming the 6 mm Hex key ends. The cold forge cranks out a spindle a second! With around 20,000 spindles made each day.

Again, very few safety measures, aside from a viewing window, are used here. My ex construction heeby jeebies were in full expression here, as the worker leans in to check the machine’s tolerances. Eeeeeee!

From the cold forge, the parts are very hot from the immense amount of friction they endure, so a cold oil bath cools them, where tolerances are checked. Then two machines: one for right- and left-handed threading presses in the threads with massive dies. One of these machines is run by a woman who’s been with MKS for 60 years, starting the day she graduated from high school!

In-House ISO Testing

From here, a couple of spindles from each batch of 2,000 will get ISO tested in-house, enduring up to 20 kilonewtons, or about 10x the ISO requirement, of force before shearing. Upon shearing, the spindle will be inspected under a microscope. Then there’s the rotation test, with 90 kg of weight pressing on a pedal spindle as it endures 1,000,000 cycles. The ISO requirement is 100,000. MKS only rotation ISO tests batches when a design changes.

Like Nitto, they’re also NJS certified, and NJS parts consume most of the factory’s energy.

Pedal Cages

MKS gets its pedal bodies die-cast in town at a local manufacturer, and from there, the various pieces are machined to attach cages and spindles. The cages, however, are die cut and pressed for embossing in-house. Elaborate designs like the Sim Works Taco Pedals require five steps to cut, stamp, perforate, and shape the pedal cages into their final form.

Assembly

From there, all the parts are loaded into crates: yellow for left-threaded, and green for right-threaded, and taken up to assembly. A machine will load the loose ball bearings, add grease, and set the initial preload on the pedals, while an employee torques them to spec before their final inspection.

The NJS pedals, however, use cartridge bearings and are fully assembled by an NJS-certified worker. He places a bearing drift into the spindle and whacks the bearing into place, listening carefully for the proper sound of a set cartridge. This worker checks each pedal multiple times before giving them a final spin in the bench vice. So much of this process is reliant on human hearing and feel. 20 years of working at MKS has made him more efficient than any machine, yet he can only assemble around 40 pairs of NJS Keirin pedals a day due to this painstaking process.

MKS Workforce

Like Nitto, MKS is grappling with an aging workforce, with 50 workers over 50 years of age. While the Japanese lifestyle has kept its national workforce young-looking, their bodies are slowing. Yuba-san explained that MKS is trying to reach a younger generation, enticing them to move to the area and work for the brand. It’s working, with the Tokyo College of Design providing some eager applicants, as well as people from Nepal and around the globe, eager to make a solid living working in industry. Currently, MKS employs 100 people, 20 of whom commute to work by bicycle.

There are many employees who have spent their entire lives working for MKS and are avid cyclists. Ito San, 65, rides a Rivendell Platypus into work every day. Her workstation is full of ephemera. Through a translation app, she smiled as she told Cari that she started riding a track bike at age 50 and was hooked on the feeling riding a bike gave her. She was assembling Keirin toe straps that day, including the buckles, and was keen to pause for a portrait.

Marketshare

Unlike Nitto, which only makes bicycle parts, around 60% of MKS production goes to the automotive industry. Japanese auto manufacturers will contract out things like seat brackets or headrests to MKS. This leaves around 40% of its output going wholly to MKS pedals. Over the past three years, the bicycle sector has grown, picking up a 10% dip in automotive work demand.

Shiny Parts from Greasy Machines

I used to think MKS pedals, like Nitto handlebars, were expensive, compared to others on the market. Yet, unlike those other pedals, they never died. If they got too loose, a simple box wrench would have them spinning like new again, and maybe a fresh repacking of grease every five years. The smell of machine oil and grease coated the machines, designed for creating some of the shiniest, prettiest pedals in the world. These acrid-smelling halls spawn perfection. Literal products of legacy from a brand that has perfected its craft over generations. I’ll never look at my MKS pedals the same again.

The Radavist x Slow Spin Society

As The Radavist celebrates its 20th anniversary of covering cycling communities, we wanted to partner with the next generation of cycling media on a lifelong dream trip of mine. We’ve featured Paul from Slow Spin Society on the website before. As a wearer of many hats – Paul also works for Sim Works as its Euro branch and was gracious enough to act as our Japanese translator during the trip – Paul is always balancing his job at Sim Works with Slow Spin. As we chatted about what a possible collaboration could look like, we landed on the idea of storytelling and interviews.

Paul wanted to focus on interviewing people at MKS, mostly the younger people, about how they got involved in working in manufacturing.

Roll on over to Slow Spin Society to read Paul’s interviews!

Fewer, Better Things

Throughout my life, I’ve strived to own fewer, better things, biting the bullet on products with an inherent value add, supporting makers and manufacturers who, against the late capitalist demands for 5% YOY growth, stayed the course and never relented. Never again will I look at a chromed spindle with black anodized cages and think: “those are too expensive.” Instead, I’ll rewrite my brain’s coding with “those pedals will outlive me.”

Pedals. They’re so simple and yet are desideratum to the functionality of the almighty bicycle. Incredulous commentators might not believe it when I say it, so it’s my job to showcase the process so that value might be perceived, no matter where the viewer may be.

I wanted to extend a special thanks to Yuba-san for showing us around and for bringing MKS into the Bespoked fold, supporting the world’s largest framebuilder showcase. I’d also like to personally thank Tanaka-san from Circles and Sim Works for believing in our work over here and supporting us through these stories. And to Paul from Slow Spin Society for his willingness and eagerness to collaborate. Miss you, friends!
